units.translation: They use two forms of the tragic genitive, with no distinction between dialogue and lyric: one Attic νεώς [of the ship], where the meter either allows or demands an iamb, the other ναός [of the ship], for which scribes sometimes substituted the Ionic form νηός [of the ship], which they knew from Homer.
The former form
There are two examples of the dative
There are four examples of the accusative ναῦν [ship]

The Attic form of the nominative plural is νῆες [ships], not ναῦς [ships], about which there is an explicit rule of Phrynichus, Ecl. p. 170. But since the tragedians said ναός [of the ship] and ναΐ [to the ship], it was consistent that they should say νᾶες [ships], not νῆες [ships], which has been wrongly introduced at Pers. 417 Ἑλληνικαί τε νῆες [and Greek ships] and Suppl. 734 νῆες ὡς ὠκύπτεροι ἥκουσι [ships come like swift-winged].

The legitimate form of the genitive is νεῶν [of the ships]: the other form ναῶν [of the ships] the tragedians do not use unless the meter demands it, about which Blomfield, after Brunck, judged correctly in his note on Pers. 389; it is sometimes wrongly introduced by scribes for νεῶν [of the ships], as at Pers. 340 ὁ πᾶς ἀριθμὸς ἐς τριακάδας δέκα | ναῶν [the whole number into ten thirties of ships], where Brunck has νεῶν [of the ships].
Dative Pers. 338
The legitimate form of the accusative is not νῆας [ships], which Phrynichus explicitly criticizes in the cited passage, but ναῦς [ships].
τύχη δὲ σωτὴρ ναῦν θέλουσ᾽ ἐφέζετο [and fortune the savior sat upon the willing ship], corrupted from ναυστολοῦσ᾽ [conveying by ship], which Casaubon restored.
A Greek ship.
Every ship was rowed.

Correctly νᾶες [ships] at Pers. 560 νᾶες μὲν ἄγαγον, τοτοῖ, νᾶες δ᾽ ἀπώλεσαν, τοτοῦ, ὁμοπτέροισιν ἐμβολαῖς [ships brought them, alas, and ships destroyed them, alas, with like-winged attacks].
The three-banked ships perished, ships without ships.
σέλμασι | ναῶν ἐπενθορόντες [leaping upon the decks of the ships], where νεῶν [of the ships] is correct in some copies.
At the beginning of a trimeter ναῶν ἄνακτες [lords of ships], where Brunck has νεῶν [of the ships].
ναῶν ἔδωκε κῦδος Ἑλλησιν μάχης [of ships he gave glory to the Greeks of the battle], where in some copies νηῶν [of the ships], in others correctly νεῶν [of the ships].
The same diversity of reading at 480 ναῶν γε ταγοὶ τῶν λελειμμένων σύδην [leaders of the ships of those left behind in a rush].
But correctly, as the meter demands, ναῶν [of the ships] at ib. 19 ἐπὶ ναῶν [upon the ships].
